newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac uses Europe to reassert battered power.
newsitem.headline: Chirac uses Europe to reassert battered power.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, his authority battered by his centre-right coalition's election defeat, is using his constitutional role in foreign policy to assert his residual power over the new left-wing government.

Chirac stepped into a row over a pact limiting budget deficits of countries that join the planned single European currency on Tuesday to try out his new, self-proclaimed role of "guarantor of France's European commitments".

While supporting Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's drive to add a pledge to coordinate European Union economic policies for growth and jobs to the pact negotiated in Dublin last year, Chirac reminded the government of the need to stick to the timetable for approving the deal next week.
He was effectively slapping down European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici, who had stressed the government wanted a real delay to study the pact and that would take longer than a week.
In doing so, aides said the conservative Gaullist president was upholding the principles he had enunciated before the election: France must speak with one voice and keep its word in Europe.

Not everyone was convinced. The financial daily Les Echos headlined its edition "France speaks with two voices before the European summit", and the popular France-Soir screamed: "Gentle cohabitation didn't last long; things are getting heavy."

Analysts said it was in Chirac's interest to help Jospin win an agreement to "balance" the stability pact with economic and employment clauses at next week's Amsterdam summit and prevent the negotiation from overrunning and causing a European crisis.

The president could claim a shared French victory and suggest his role was vital in persuading Paris' uneasy German partners to make the necessary gestures for the sake of their grand project of economic and monetary union (EMU).

"He has played his part very skilfully by recalling that France's signature must be honoured, while echoing the government's call for an anti-unemployment, social element alongside the punitive measures in the stability pact," France-Soir editorialist Bernard Morrot said.
Jospin has effectively muted election campaign rhetoric attacking the fines for budget overspending that are the core of the stability pact, negotiated at Bonn's insistence.

But the Socialists may be able to claim to have achieved in a week what their centre-right predecessors failed to win in last December's Dublin negotiations, an EU "economic government" to balance the independent European central bank, and a shift of emphasis from a purely monetary to a social Europe.
In fact, diplomats said, that change may be largely verbal and it reflects a shift to the centre-left in several European countries, notably Britain as well as France.

Government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann sought to quash any suggestion of a clash between Chirac and Jospin, saying there was no divergence between the two men on EMU and their preparation for the Amsterdam summit was harmonious.
Symbolically, the president and prime minister agreed on a design for the euro coins which France will propose to its EU partners, Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn reported.
"On this European side of the coin, France, as is normal, has spoken with one voice," he quipped.
Like the euro banknotes, the coins will have a common design on one side and a national symbol on the other.

The French constitution is ambiguous on the foreign policy powers of the president and government. The president signs and is responsible for upholding treaties, giving him an extensive say in European affairs, but the prime minister "determines and conducts the policy of the nation".
The head of state traditionally represents France at EU summits, giving him a psychological protocol advantage over his colleagues at the table, who are mostly prime ministers.
Jospin plans to attend the Amsterdam summit alongside Chirac, as former conservative prime minister Edouard Balladur did with the late president Francois Mitterrand in 1993.
This week's euro diplomacy has shown that although his power is seriously diminished, Chirac will be more than a lame duck.
